slides: Now let's learn about tangents to a circle. It's a short lesson, with two rules that come up a lot.

slides.say: A tangent is a straight line that touches the circle at one point only. It doesn't go inside the circle.
at: A tangent is a straight line
that touches the circle at one point

slides.say: If the line were a little further in, it would go through the circle and cut it at two points. Then the part inside the circle would be a chord.
And if the line passed outside, it wouldn't touch the circle at all. It's just a line.
at: And if the line passed outside

slides.say: So our tangent touches the circle at one point only. This point is called the point of tangency.
Now a very, very important rule. The radius is perpendicular to the tangent at the point of tangency.
at: Now a very, very important rule

slides.say: Here the tangent touches the circle at D. When I draw a radius to the point of tangency, from O to D, I get a ninety-degree angle between the radius and the tangent.

Why? The tangent touches the circle only at D. Every other point of the tangent is outside the circle, so it's farther from O than the radius. So D is the point of the tangent that is closest to O. And we know the shortest way from a point to a line is the perpendicular. So O D is perpendicular to the tangent.
at: Every other point of the tangent
So D is the point of the tangent

slides.say: It doesn't matter where the tangent touches. Here, and here, the radius to the point of tangency is always perpendicular to the tangent.
This rule is used very often. A tangent gives us a right angle when we join O to its touching point. So every time you see a circle question with tangents, draw the radius to the point of tangency.

slides.say: Let's see it in numbers. The radius of this circle is five, and P is thirteen away from the center. P D is a tangent. How long is it?
A tangent, so I draw the radius to the point of tangency, O D. It's five, and the angle at D is ninety. Now join O to P. That's thirteen.
So O D P is a right triangle, and thirteen is its hypotenuse, because it's across from the right angle. By Pythagoras, five squared plus P D squared is thirteen squared.
at: So O D P is a right triangle

slides.say: Twenty-five plus P D squared is a hundred sixty-nine. To get P D squared alone, we take twenty-five off both sides. So P D squared is a hundred sixty-nine minus twenty-five, which is a hundred forty-four. A length is positive, so P D is twelve.
We can also spot it with a triple. Five and thirteen should remind you of the triple five, twelve, thirteen.
From the same point P, we can draw a second tangent to the circle, on the other side. It touches the circle at E.

Now let's look at the second rule. From the same point outside the circle, the two tangent segments are equal. Here they're P D and P E. Each one starts at P and stops at its touching point. Why are they equal? Look at the two right triangles. The first one is O D P.

slides.say: The second one is O E P. Its radius O E is also five, and it has the same hypotenuse, O P, thirteen. So Pythagoras gives the same thing, and P E is twelve too.
